case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old Asian-Indian male was referred for evaluation of a slow-growing conjunctival mass in the right eye over 27 years. There was no pain or discharge. He had previously undergone partial lamellar sclerouvectomy (PLSU) 30 years prior for ciliochoroidal melanoma in the right eye, followed by pars plana vitrectomy and scleral buckle 1 year later for retinal detachment (RD) with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) in the right eye. On examination, visual acuity was no light perception OD and 20/25 OS, with intraocular pressures of 33 mm Hg and 17 mm Hg in the right and left eyes, respectively. Examination results of the left eye were normal. Anterior segment examination in the right eye revealed thin conjunctiva with a nontender multilobular pigmented lesion in the superonasal quadrant (Figure 1), underlying Tenon fascia and surrounded by prominent episcleral feeder vessels (Figure 1, yellow arrowhead). The cornea showed nasal epithelial defect and flat anterior chamber with cataract and iris neovascularization. There was no view to the posterior segment. Ultrasonography revealed a homogenous echodensity within the vitreous cavity (Figure 1insets, asterisks) measuring 21 mm in thickness, along with an echolucent episcleral mass (Figure 1insets, arrowhead) 7 mm thick. In addition, spontaneous vascular pulsations (SVP) were noted within the intraocular component (Video).

options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits

case_info.answer: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits
case_info.caption: Imaging of the right eye at 30 years’ follow-up after partial lamellar sclerouvectomy. External photography documenting a superonasal, multilobulated, pigmented lesion with episcleral feeder vessels (arrowhead) located under Tenon fascia. Ultrasonography (inset images) showing homogenous echodensity within the globe (asterisks) with an echolucent extrascleral component (inset, arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

dialogue_history.text: I agree that a tissue diagnosis is essential, but incisional biopsy of a pigmented conjunctival lesion with prominent feeder vessels and a history of intraocular melanoma carries a high risk of seeding tumor cells and causing significant hemorrhage. Given the ultrasonographic findings of a large intraocular mass with spontaneous vascular pulsations, a metastatic or recurrent melanoma is likely, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) under ultrasound guidance would be a safer initial diagnostic step to confirm malignancy before definitive management.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 3.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.caption: Imaging of the right eye at 30 years’ follow-up after partial lamellar sclerouvectomy. External photography documenting a superonasal, multilobulated, pigmented lesion with episcleral feeder vessels (arrowhead) located under Tenon fascia. case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

External photography documenting a superonasal, multilobulated, pigmented lesion with episcleral feeder vessels (arrowhead) located under Tenon fascia. case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 70-year-old Asian-Indian male was referred for evaluation of a slow-growing conjunctival mass in the right eye over 27 years. There was no pain or discharge. He had previously undergone partial lamellar sclerouvectomy (PLSU) 30 years prior for ciliochoroidal melanoma in the right eye, followed by pars plana vitrectomy and scleral buckle 1 year later for retinal detachment (RD) with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) in the right eye. On examination, visual acuity was no light perception OD and 20/25 OS, with intraocular pressures of 33 mm Hg and 17 mm Hg in the right and left eyes, respectively. Examination results of the left eye were normal. Anterior segment examination in the right eye revealed thin conjunctiva with a nontender multilobular pigmented lesion in the superonasal quadrant (Figure 1), underlying Tenon fascia and surrounded by prominent episcleral feeder vessels (Figure 1, yellow arrowhead). The cornea showed nasal epithelial defect and flat anterior chamber with cataract and iris neovascularization. There was no view to the posterior segment. Ultrasonography revealed a homogenous echodensity within the vitreous cavity (Figure 1insets, asterisks) measuring 21 mm in thickness, along with an echolucent episcleral mass (Figure 1insets, arrowhead) 7 mm thick. In addition, spontaneous vascular pulsations (SVP) were noted within the intraocular component (Video).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{

  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"

Given the history of a slow-growing conjunctival mass and the concerning features observed, including the multilobulated pigmented lesion with vascularization, the most appropriate next step in management is a C. Incisional biopsy. This will help to clarify the nature of the lesion, particularly considering the patient's previous history of ciliochoroidal melanoma and the potential for recurrence or secondary malignancy. Imaging could be useful, but obtaining a definitive diagnosis through biopsy is critical at this stage.

I agree that a tissue diagnosis is essential, but incisional biopsy of a pigmented conjunctival lesion with prominent feeder vessels and a history of intraocular melanoma carries a high risk of seeding tumor cells and causing significant hemorrhage. Given the ultrasonographic findings of a large intraocular mass with spontaneous vascular pulsations, a metastatic or recurrent melanoma is likely, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) under ultrasound guidance would be a safer initial diagnostic step to confirm malignancy before definitive management.

Your point regarding the risks of incisional biopsy is noted, particularly concerning tumor seeding. However, an incisional biopsy, particularly if well-planned, can still be performed safely to obtain a definitive diagnosis. The presence of pronounced feeder vessels does warrant caution, but my inclination remains towards direct tissue diagnosis since it can provide clarity on the lesion's nature, which is vital for appropriate management.

While a well-planned incisional biopsy is possible, the key issue is the large underlying intraocular mass with vascular pulsations, which suggests a high-flow tumor. An incisional approach through this vascular bed risks severe, uncontrolled bleeding. A safer strategy is to first obtain a cytologic diagnosis via FNAB, which can confirm melanoma recurrence without the morbidity of an open procedure.

While I acknowledge the risks associated with incisional biopsy in this case, the need for a definitive diagnosis remains paramount. However, your emphasis on the safety of fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) is notable and may indeed provide a less invasive means of obtaining cytological material. I am willing to reconsider my approach to either proceed with FNAB first or potentially plan for a careful incisional biopsy under controlled circumstances, depending on further imaging or assessment of vascularity prior to any intervention.

That's a reasonable pivot. Given the complex vascularity and the patient's monocular status, starting with FNAB under ultrasound guidance is prudent to confirm the suspected recurrent melanoma with minimal risk. If cytology is diagnostic, it directly guides definitive therapy—often enucleation—without needing a more morbid incisional procedure.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

External photography documenting a superonasal, multilobulated, pigmented lesion with episcleral feeder vessels (arrowhead) located under Tenon fascia. case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

case_info.caption: Imaging of the right eye at 30 years’ follow-up after partial lamellar sclerouvectomy. External photography documenting a superonasal, multilobulated, pigmented lesion with episcleral feeder vessels (arrowhead) located under Tenon fascia. Ultrasonography (inset images) showing homogenous echodensity within the globe (asterisks) with an echolucent extrascleral component (inset, arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Extraocular extension of recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma B. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and orbits The preferred treatment modalities for uveal melanoma (UM) include plaque radiotherapy or enucleation, depending on tumor extent.1However, PLSU has also been a reasonable procedure for anteriorly located iridociliochoroidal melanoma for several decades.1-3This technique of local surgical resection involves creating a hinged, partial-thickness scleral flap to excise the tumor. It avoids radiation complications, such as radiation retinopathy, maculopathy, and papillopathy, as well as the visual penalties associated with enucleation.2However, in the early postoperative period (48 hours to 8 weeks), PLSU is associated with RD in 2% to 12% of patients, with VH in 27% to 29% of patients, and with local recurrence in 5% to 11% of patients.2,3 Much like the initial diagnosis of UM, the diagnosis of tumor recurrence is made by clinical observation and presents with either-edge recurrence, increase in thickness, or new orange pigment.4Posterior segment examination is often limited due to various postsurgical findings, including total RD, VH, or dense cataract, as in this case. In this scenario, certain ultrasonographic features played a crucial role. Apart from the echogenicity and morphology of the intraocular structures, ultrasonography was important in detecting a solid mass with SVP, seen as localized pulsating figures within the mass (Video).5These figures denote intrinsic vessels and are pathognomonic of a viable intraocular tumor, as opposed to VH, which would be inert, without pulsations.6Although reported in literature, SVP are often overlooked. On the other hand, changes in Doppler ultrasonography are correlated with tumor regression, specifically a decrease in peak systolic frequency following plaque radiotherapy as well as Cyberknife (Accuray) radiotherapy.7,8 In this case, SVP was critical in diagnosing tumor recurrence, ruling out postsurgical scleral ectasia and VH. Therefore, scleral patch graft or observation are inappropriate management options. Incisional biopsy is not ideal for melanoma, as it would risk tumor dissemination across the ocular surface, eyelid, and orbit. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging performed to explore the extent of orbital tumor involvement showed the mass to be hyperintense on fat-suppressed, T1-weighted images (Figure 2) and hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2inset), suggestive of orbital melanoma recurrence.5Limited exenteration with enucleation was performed to remove the globe and extraocular extension in 1 specimen. Histopathology confirmed recurrent ciliochoroidal melanoma with extraocular extension. UM recurrence can be slow and mimic an ocular surface lesion externally or VH ultrasonographically. Fortunately, tumor recurrence following plaque radiotherapy is rare. However, in the early postoperative period, RD is seen in 1.5% and VH in 4% of patients.9,10Ultrasonography focusing on SVP is a relevant clinical tool for tumor detection. These findings, along with gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance images, are valuable surrogates for detecting tumor recurrence. At 2-month follow-up, the enucleated socket was healed. The patient was planned for a custom-fit prosthesis and orbital radiotherapy. Periodic systemic surveillance for metastatic disease was advised.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

A 70-year-old Asian-Indian male was referred for evaluation of a slow-growing conjunctival mass in the right eye over 27 years. There was no pain or discharge. Ultrasonography revealed a homogenous echodensity within the vitreous cavity (Figure 1insets, asterisks) measuring 21 mm in thickness, along with an echolucent episcleral mass (Figure 1insets, arrowhead) 7 mm thick. In addition, spontaneous vascular pulsations (SVP) were noted within the intraocular component (Video).

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.6. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.
